props.title: The Tingler

sections.content: The Tingler (1959) stands as William Castle's masterpiece of theatrical gimmickry and B-movie innovation. Castle installed vibrating devices called "Percepto" under select theater seats that buzzed during key scenes, creating a literal spine-tingling experience when the parasitic creature appeared. This pioneering mix of film and physical audience interaction paved the way for later theatrical experiments like Earthquake (1974) with Sensurround and The Blair Witch Project's (1999) groundbreaking viral marketing. Castle's showmanship transformed B-movie horror into an immersive event.

sections.content: Vincent Price delivers a deliciously hammy performance as Dr. Warren Chapin, who discovers that fear manifests physically as a creature attached to the spine. The film's practical effects, while dated, showcase the ingenuity of 1950s horror filmmaking. The creature design - a centipede-like monster - draws from Universal's creature features like Creature from the Black Lagoon (1954) while adding its own twisted biology. The premise that screaming defeats the monster cleverly encouraged audience participation, making viewers complicit in the action.

Beyond its gimmicks, The Tingler pushed boundaries with its hallucinatory LSD sequence (one of cinema's first drug trips), a bathtub scene featuring blood in color while the rest remained black and white, and meta-theatrical moments where the creature "attacks" the projection booth. These innovative techniques influenced later horror meta-commentary like Demons (1985) and Popcorn (1991). SUBHEAD: The Legacy of William Castle's Showmanship

movies.title: Strait-Jacket
movies.slug: Castle teams with Joan Crawford for an axe-murder thriller with theater ushers wielding cardboard axes

sections.content: Castle's promotional stunts for The Tingler included insurance policies against "death by fright" and nurses stationed in theaters. This carnival barker approach to cinema influenced later directors like John Waters, who used "Odorama" scratch-and-sniff cards for Polyester (1981), and Robert Rodriguez's "Aromascope" in Spy Kids 4 (2011). Even modern immersive experiences like 4DX theaters owe a debt to Castle's pioneering fusion of film and physical sensation.
